resources.string: Three views of normal peripheral ganglia. Cell sizes, spacing and animation timing are schematic.

In a dorsal root ganglion, a single stem leaves the sensory neuron soma and divides at a T-junction. An impulse from the periphery runs into the central branch of the same pseudounipolar neuron, toward the spinal cord. It does not need to pass through the soma or cross a synapse inside the ganglion.

A preganglionic axon from the central nervous system ends inside the ganglion. Its terminal signals across a synaptic cleft to a different neuron, here on a dendrite. An impulse can then travel along that postganglionic neuron toward its target.

In a dorsal root ganglion, flattened satellite glial cells form a thin sheath around a sensory neuron soma. They help regulate its immediate extracellular environment, including local potassium levels. The highlighted space is exaggerated for clarity. This sheath is neither axonal myelin nor a neuronal relay.

Sympathetic preganglionic fibers arise from thoracic and upper lumbar spinal cord segments, commonly T1–L2. Only representative connections are shown.
The two trunks of linked ganglia lie beside the vertebral column. Fibers can synapse at their entry level, travel up or down the trunk, or pass through to a prevertebral ganglion.
Parasympathetic fibers leave the brainstem in cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X. The vagus (X) reaches targets in the chest and much of the abdomen. Routes are grouped here.
Parasympathetic fibers from spinal cord segments S2–S4 travel in the pelvic splanchnic nerves toward the distal bowel and pelvic organs.
Parasympathetic fibers typically synapse close to or within the target organ. The short segment beyond this example ganglion represents the postganglionic fiber.
